This dysregulation of ion transport, particularly impacting Sodium-Potassium ATPase activity, results in the common phenotypes of hypertension and hyperkalemia seen in both diseases.

#### 1. pseudohypoaldosteronism type 2C  —  Tier 3 — Moderate / Emerging  (fitness 0.414)
**Link type:** shared pathway (Reactome:R-HSA-2672351)

**Proposed mechanism:** WNK1 (HGNC:12744) —INCREASES→ SPAK/OSR1 kinases (HGNC:11157); SPAK/OSR1 kinases (HGNC:11157) —INCREASES→ Phosphorylation of NCC and NKCC (REACT:R-HSA-8935440); Phosphorylation of NCC and NKCC (REACT:R-HSA-8935440) —INCREASES→ Sodium retention (REACT:R-HSA-109573); Phosphorylation of NCC and NKCC (REACT:R-HSA-8935440) —DECREASES→ Potassium excretion (REACT:R-HSA-109574); Sodium retention (REACT:R-HSA-109573) —LEADS_TO→ Hypertension (HP:0000822); Potassium excretion (REACT:R-HSA-109574) —LEADS_TO→ Hyperkalemia (HP:0011074); Sodium retention (REACT:R-HSA-109573) —DISRUPTS→ Sodium-Potassium ATPase activity (GO:0005372); Sodium-Potassium ATPase activity (GO:0005372) —LEADS_TO→ Hypertension (HP:0000822). Gain-of-function mutations in WNK1 lead to increased WNK1 kinase activity, which in turn activates SPAK/OSR1 kinases. These activated kinases phosphorylate and increase the activity of the NCC and NKCC transporters, leading to increased sodium reabsorption and decreased potassium excretion. This dysregulation of ion transport, particularly impacting Sodium-Potassium ATPase activity, results in the common phenotypes of hypertension and hyperkalemia seen in both diseases.

**How to falsify it:** Identification of loss-of-function mutations in WNK1 in patients with either MONDO:0014019 or pseudohypoaldosteronism type 2C, or evidence that the shared phenotypes are driven by entirely distinct molecular pathways not involving WNK1-mediated ion transport regulation. _(variant: rs1436693092)_

**Why it matters:** Understanding the shared mechanism involving WNK1 and ion transporter dysregulation in both conditions could lead to the development of targeted therapies for hypertension and hyperkalemia, potentially benefiting patients with either disease. For instance, targeting the downstream effects of WNK1 activation could offer therapeutic avenues.
